articles.content: EXCLUSIVE: Tony Lipp and Dara Gordon have joined Entertainment 360 as partners. Lipp will also join the management board, and Gordon will lead the New York office. articles.content: At SCAD Film Festival, the directors of this year’s animated feature contenders are making films not aimed at children. The MPA gave “ Wildwood ” a PG-13 for “strong fantasy violence/bloody images, thematic material, suicide-related material, brief partial nudity and language,” which is a mouthful for any movie and an especially wild one for a stop-motion picture about a girl hunting for her kidnapped baby brother. It’s the first PG-13 in Laika’s 17 years as a feature studio, and at 130 minutes, it ties the record for the longest English-language animated film ever made. Travis Knight, who runs the Portland, Ore., studio and directed “Wildwood,” didn’t land there by accident. Anyone who remembers how dark the back half of “Kubo and the Two Strings” got probably isn’t shocked he went this far. articles.content: I asked Ellen Burstyn where a Grammy would go, if she ever won one. She stands up to show me. “I wonder if I took my iPad off the stand and walked you into my office, where they all are,” she says, immediately reaching for it over a video Zoom. articles.summary: The conversation at IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit also touched on the franchise's incredible longevity and resonance in our current political climate.
articles.content: AI is continuing to be implemented in the post-production stages of studio films, though “Hunger Games” franchise producer Nina Jacobson still views it as a “tool for artists” and “not a substitute” for them. During a conversation with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang at IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles Jacobson said the team used AI approximations of actors to test out new line readings for the upcoming prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Those lines would then be recorded with the cast in traditional automated dialogue replacement process. “We just finished [post-production], fairly recently, on ‘Sunrise on the Reaping.’ We used [AI] very specifically as a tool — within production, within post-production — while, at the same time, never using it to ever replace any of our artists or anything you see onscreen,” Jacobson said. “When you have ADR you want try out, you used to either have the editor getting in there with the lines you wanted … Just for something you’re trying out that you might not even keep. [AI] is a great tool to use ADR.” Related Stories Tom Skerritt, ‘Alien’ and ‘M*A*S*H’ Star, Dies at 93 Cinema Eye Honors Unveil Nominees for 2027’s Best Documentary Films and Series Jacobson went on to explain how the technology has relatively limited applications for her, none of which find their way onto the screen. “They can duplicate a voice. You can have the thing that you want to go get, or do a slug that actually looks like what you want … But we would still never use it because it’s not our actors,” she continued. “We’d go to our writer for the dialogue. Sarandos, who won by a vote of acclamation, succeeds Bob Daly, who held that position for the last 17 years. “Ted Sarandos is one of the world’s most dynamic industry executives and a passionate movie lover,” Daly tells us. “It’s my honor to hand him the gavel to lead AFI into an even greater future.” Adds Sarandos, “I’m honored to carry on the stewardship of an organization that celebrates film and television arts. articles.title: Don’t Get the Wrong Idea About ‘The Dropout’
articles.summary: Watching Elizabeth Holmes watch "The Dropout" in "You Can See Everything" may leave viewers questioning the merits of Amanda Seyfried's Emmy-winning limited series. But its bona fides are stronger than ever — and the movie knows it.
articles.content: [Editor’s note: The following article contains spoilers for “ You Can See Everything .”] Among the snippets of “ The Dropout ” shown in “You Can See Everything,” Amanda Seyfried dancing to “I’m in a Hurry (And Don’t Know Why)” is by far my favorite. The scene sees Seyfried portraying a 17-year-old Elizabeth Holmes as she stares intently at a poster of Steve Jobs, semi-rhythmically churning her arms and letting herself be seduced by the Apple inventor’s image. As she bends and sways to Alabama’s country-rock classic (in the first of many dance scenes scattered throughout “The Dropout”), it’s as if her ambition is trying to shake free from her body. Her focus shifts, from implicit personal frustrations to an idea sparked by her idol, but it never wavers. She’s determined. Driven. Her famously imposing peepers bulge with excitement. Related Stories ‘The Debut’ Is the Go-to Festival Crowdpleaser as Jesse Eisenberg’s Musical Comedy Launches at Virginia Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Neon to Present Free ‘Once Upon a Time in Harlem’ New York City Screenings In the context of the film , the scene is ridiculous. On a computer screen in front of the real Holmes is an exaggerated version of the Theranos founder, who’s watching along with her husband, Billy Evans, and documentarian, Nathan Fielder . When Fielder asks, “Did you really do that?” the answer is a foregone conclusion: Of course she didn’t. And if she did, she would never admit to it now. In the context of the show, the scene is also ridiculous. The exaggerated version of Holmes isn’t meant to be a reenactment, like what Fielder orchestrates with Seyfried later in the movie. It’s a character, used to illustrate fundamental truths about the elusive tech founder and convicted fraudster: She’s obsessed with changing the world, she can’t wait to get started, and — perhaps most importantly — she doesn’t know why. ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on Spending 16 Years to Create His Stop-Motion “Masterpiece”
articles.content: The filmmaker and Nike scion poured untold millions into his critically acclaimed "grand experiment." But he knows the real test is yet to come. Travis Knight looks like a man who has returned from battle. In reality, we’re talking many (fictional) battles, scripted and designed and meticulously staged and shot over 16 years. On a scalding afternoon in Beverly Hills, the 53-year-old studio chief and director has flown in from London, where he’s just completed postproduction on Wildwood , which could safely be called his life’s work. “It’s been a part of my life for more than half my career,” says Knight, Wildwood ‘s director and producer. “So I’m going through a little bit of a depression. It’s this thing that occupies so much of your time and your thoughts and your emotions — and when you’re done with it, it’s like, ‘What do I do with all this?’ ” He comes at all of this from an unusual angle, as both a bottom-line-minded studio chief — he’s been running his independent animation company, Laika, for about 20 years — and an artist standing in defiant opposition to certain industry headwinds. He hasn’t sat for a longform interview in years, mainly because of the intensive demands of Wildwood ‘s 231 weeks of production. And so, as we settle into a restaurant overlooking L.A., we’re arriving at the part he’s less comfortable with — selling the thing. “I find myself essentially performing all the time,” he says of his role as Laika figurehead. Before L.A., he stopped in Telluride and Annecy, France, for Wildwood promotional pop-ups; the film’s world premiere then brought him back to London. The movie at last hits theaters Oct. 23. articles.title: James Bond Screen Tests to Happen This Weekend: Finalists Emerge for Next 007 Movie
articles.content: Tomorrow never dies. But for all actors except one, the dream of being the next James Bond will likely die this week. And that is due to — finally! — a very select group of actors getting in front of cameras to screen test for the role of British agent 007. According to several sources, Callum Turner , who recently starred in the rom-com One Night Only , and Slow Horses actor Jack Lowden are said to be in the mix for the screen tests, which are taking place in London this weekend. They could begin as early as Friday, according to two sources. It is unclear who else may be testing. Sources said at least three actors are part of the action but another source says up to five may be putting on the tux to see how it fits. articles.content: In recent years, interest in fan fiction has risen right alongside Hollywood’s persistent investment in adapting pre-existing IP. Novels and plays in the book-to-screen pipeline are now simply another part of the ecosystem, and it seems fanfic as a viable IP isn’t just the latest trend, but an industry-wide move to appeal directly to pre-existing fanbases and trust narratives that have been tried and tested repeatedly. Fanfic — the practice of fans writing fiction based on pre-existing work and characters, often with relationships that differ from the original canon — has grown so popular and expansive that it’s impossible to ignore. Contemporary fanfic is said to have originated in the late 1960s, when the “Star Trek” fandom wrote fanzines; a popular pairing was James T. Kirk and Spock. While AO3’s readership continues to grow exponentially (November 2025 saw over 146.6 million weekly page views more than the previous November), fanfic is also breaking into mainstream culture, with people openly declaring themselves fanfic readers and even celebs weighing in on fanfic . articles.title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Hopes People “See The Danger” In GenAI, Calls It “Antithetical” To Laika’s Work
articles.content: As Laika debuts its latest stop-motion animation, Travis Knight is standing firmly against generative AI . The Wildwood director and Laika CEO explained that GenAI “is antithetical to everything that we are at this studio,” also emphasizing that he hopes people “see the danger” in the technology’s potential as much as the “value.” “But all of these things have meaning and value when you put them in the hands of an artist,” he told The Verge . “When the technology is doing the work of the artist, that’s a different proposition. And that’s something that I am steadfastly against, because there is no humanity in what comes out of the other side of that. Knight continued, “When you’ve ingested the material that an artist has actually created, and then regurgitate it in a different way, there’s no soul, there’s no spirit, there’s no humanity behind it. articles.title: Trump Says Google CEO Rejected His Request to Rename Atlantic Ocean on Google Maps
articles.content: President Donald Trump , who has already renamed two bodies of water after America, said he would like to redub the Atlantic Ocean as well — but that the CEO of Google pushed back on the idea. At a rally at Clemson University in South Carolina Tuesday evening, Trump told the crowd, “So we have a lake. And we have a gulf. Now we need a river, and we need an ocean.” Trump continued: “I only like two oceans: the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. I’m not gonna put either ‘Trump’ or ‘America’ on any other ocean but these two.” Related Stories U.S. Bank and Visa Present An Evening With Jessica Alba in Partnership With Variety 'Line of Fire' Gets Full 18-Episode Season Order at NBC Last year, Trump declared that the Gulf of Mexico would henceforth be known as the “Gulf of America.” Then this August, amid a trade feud with Canada, he ordered Lake Ontario to be now called “Lake America.” Popular on Variety Trump said he “seriously looked at” renaming the Atlantic Ocean and called Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet and Google, to ask about whether Google Maps would rename the Atlantic. “I said, ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean. Please don’t ask us to do that.” Trump said after the conversation with Pichai, he would “probably pass” on trying to rename the Atlantic Ocean. articles.summary: In her latest documentary, ‘Miss Representation: Rise Up,’ the filmmaker and First Partner of California argues that tech platforms and AI tools have been weaponized to silence women’s voices.
articles.content: A lot has changed since 2011. The urgency of talking about the way women are represented in media, unfortunately, has not, according to Jennifer Siebel Newsom. The documentary filmmaker and the current First Partner of California initially tackled the subject of media’s impact on the underrepresentation of women in positions of power in her 2011 documentary Miss Representation . Victoria Hinks, the mother of a 16-year-old who died by suicide after Hinks says she became addicted to social media, also speaks for the film. Lang plays Joe McCabe, a former soldier and reclusive Texas rancher who decides to risk everything to fight back against immigration authorities after they detain a hardworking local father. Determined to reunite the farmer with his family, McCabe comes up against a hard-line immigration agent, Harvey “Hawk” Walters, played by Irish actor Jack Hudson . The film is set to shoot in Mexico. articles.summary: After dating Marcia on ‘The Brady Bunch,’ he spent three seasons turning into Captain Marvel on Saturday mornings.
articles.content: Michael Gray, who starred on the 1970s Saturday morning kids show Shazam! as Billy Batson, the teenager who in a puff of smoke turns into the superhero Captain Marvel , died Friday in Palm Desert of natural causes, a family spokesperson announced. Gray frequently graced the covers of Tiger Beat and other popular teen magazines as he landed his first series gig as a student doctor named Ronnie Collins on the first season of the 1972-74 NBC sitcom The Little People , starring Brian Keith and Shelley Fabares . Gray’s Billy had but to utter one word — “shazam” — to be transformed into Captain Marvel (played by Jackson Bostwick and then John Davey) on the live-action CBS show that aired for three seasons (1974-76). articles.title: Streaming Ratings: ‘Carrie’ Has a Bloody Good Opening Week
articles.content: Earlier Thursday, Prime Video announced a second season renewal for Carrie . Now there’s publicly available data backing up the decision. Carrie premiered as the No. 1 streaming title in the United States for the week of Oct. 5-11. The eight-episode season, a present-day update of Stephen King’s novel from showrunner Mike Flanagan, racked up 1.26 billion viewing minutes for the week (the series debuted on Oct. 7). Prime Video has been on a bit of a hot streak lately: It has had the No. 1 overall title six times in the past eight weeks of Nielsen’s streaming ratings . Reacher held the top ranking four times in August and September, giving way to spinoff Neagley in the week of Sept. 14-20 . The previous week’s top show, Wonka’s The Golden Ticket , fell off by 44 percent to 600 million viewing minutes for Netflix. It dropped out of the overall top 10 but finished sixth among original series. Ted Lasso (943 million minutes), on the other hand, scored a six-week high on Apple TV, coinciding with its season four finale on Oct. 7. Two shows got a boost from licensing deals with Netflix: Paramount+’s Mayor of Kingstown (712 million minutes) and Disney+’s Percy Jackson and the Olympians (365 million) charted after their libraries debuted on Netflix (new seasons of both, in their original homes, will premiere in the next few months). Line of Fire centers on the Hollingsworth family, whose members work in various branches of federal law enforcement and who are seemingly being targeted by an assassin. articles.title: Artists Equity’s Amy Baer on Building a Sustainable Indie Model with Movies That Don’t Star Matt Damon or Ben Affleck
articles.summary: The production label's president of film and TV discusses the newly-launched Artists Equity Independent Pictures and how to apply their unique model to smaller films.
articles.content: It can still be a struggle for people to grasp exactly what Ben Affleck and Matt Damon ‘s Artists Equity banner is all about or how it works. In some cases it’s even hard for its own leaders to articulate what gives the company its secret sauce. “I think they’re beginning to understand it, but I think that people don’t really understand the ambition and scope of this business,” Amy Baer , Artists Equity’s president of film and television and the No. 2 to Matt and Ben, told IndieWire. “It is existing to enable and preserve the art of visual storytelling,” she continued. “[Damon and Affleck] are deeply, deeply rooted in the history of film. They are cinephiles, both of them, passionate cinephiles who not only want to redefine how creatives — both in front of the camera and behind the camera — are compensated, which is obviously the foundational component of our company, the equity piece, but to also ensure that we are creating a virtuous cycle so that it can endure.” Related Stories Don’t Get the Wrong Idea About ‘The Dropout’ ‘The Debut’ Is the Go-to Festival Crowdpleaser as Jesse Eisenberg’s Musical Comedy Launches at Virginia But Baer feels her job in explaining the Artists Equity model to people just got a little easier with the launch of the company’s new independent label, Artists Equity Independent Pictures (AEIP). articles.title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Neon to Present Free ‘Once Upon a Time in Harlem’ New York City Screenings
articles.summary: The Oscar-contending documentary that captures a 1972 meeting of Harlem Renaissance luminaries will screen at three NYC venues, October 24 - 25.
articles.content: The Greaves family ‘s “ Once Upon a Time in Harlem ” is making waves in this year’s Best Documentary Feature Oscar race — and it’s about to screen for free throughout New York City this weekend. A day after Neon announced a partnership with The Guardian to expand the theatrical release of another documentary Oscar contender, “ NAZA ,” the company is now partnering with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to bring “ Once Upon a Time in Harlem ” to more audiences. Four free screenings of the film , co-directed by the late William Greaves with his son David, will roll out on Saturday, October 24, and Sunday, October 25, in New York City. The screenings will take place at the AMC Magic Johnson Harlem, Film Forum, and Film at Lincoln Center, “celebrating the legacy of the Harlem Renaissance and the enduring global power of art, culture, and creativity,” per the announcement. Our city owes a debt of gratitude to the artists of the Harlem Renaissance whose enduring legacy is still felt in every jazz club, in every gallery, and in the movement for social justice that still continues to this day.” The film premiered at Sundance before moving on to play Cannes, Telluride, Toronto, and New York, among other festivals. articles.content: There’s nothing quite like a good theme. And while that is mostly true — especially as it applies to the romance of our leads Joanne ( Kristen Bell ) and Noah ( Adam Brody ) — there’s another, darker theme lurking just underneath. articles.summary: Anton Corbijn directs the pair in a two-hander with real bite, as adapted by Joanna Murray-Smith from her devilish play "Switzerland."
articles.content: [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 14, 2026 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.] In recent years, movie audiences have fallen back in love with the whodunnit, thanks to the mighty talents of Rian Johnson and Kenneth Branagh and more. That the classic mystery subgenre would continue to stake its claim in the cinematic world is no surprise. When executed well, there’s nothing quite so fun as going for a ride that ends with a tidy, smart ending. This is who did the deed, and this is how they did it, and this is why. Related Stories Is Fan Fiction Really the Next Frontier in IP? When VFX and Practical Sets Work Together, Sometimes You Invent New Cameras Iconic novelist Patricia Highsmith was far more concerned with the final part of that particular answer. Why. The creator of Tom Ripley wasn’t very interested in untangling who — we always knew who! — but what made him (or her other, often less popular creations) tick. Whydunnit, as it were. And Highsmith’s own compulsion toward building twisted, twisty characters is given fresh life (new blood?) in Anton Corbijn’s clever “A Talent for Murder,” adapted by playwright Joanna Murray-Smith, who first constructed this slice of fiction for her play “Switzerland.” Built on the barest of real facts — like that Highsmith was a prickly customer who spent her final years basically holed up in a Swiss home that people called “the bunker” — Murray-Smith spins out her own story of psychological trauma and maybe, just maybe , actual murder. Starring a wonderfully terrifying Dame Helen Mirren as this fictionalized Highsmith, the film opens with a clearly out-of-his-depth (or is he?) young editor making his way to the bunker in question.
